messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: new commit/push policy?
parts:
We've been getting lots of broken pushes
lately (missing tests, missing doc, code in
the wrong namespace, etc.) I'm as guilty as
anyone here, if not more so, so I hope nobody
takes this as an implied criticism.

The problem will probably only get worse as we have more
developers as we haven't made our coding standards
particularly clear.

What I'm wondering is whether we should go
to a system where we pull request rather than
push ourselves and where there's a forced code
review by someone other than the person issuing
the pull request.

Thoughts?

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new commit/push policy?
parts:
I'm torn. More formal code review would probably be good for us and
getting into the habit would make it easier for other people to join
the process (as we would be more used to the "pull request" workflow).
That said, for some cases it seems excessive. E.G., I pushed some
commits which made changes to the printed output of BFGS...hardly in
need of code review.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: new commit/push policy?
parts:
On Wednesday, May 1, 2013 3:40:02 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
What I'm wondering is whether we should go
to a system where we pull request rather than
push ourselves and where there's a forced code
review by someone other than the person issuing
the pull request.

I feel that there are a lot of areas of the Stan code that only one person knows well. In that case, the code reviewer might not be able to do that great a job, and the person who has a lot of commits might be slowed down.

Part of the problem is that too many commits are going to the master branch too soon. Like "I'll push the code now and the tests / doc / etc. later". Part of the problem is that we don't enforce a push hook that runs test-unit. I think Bob sent an email a couple of weeks ago about the 5 steps needed to add something to Stan, but we don't really have any formal guidelines.

Ben

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: new commit/push policy?
parts:
My vote is for pull requests. I'm against process as much as everyone else, but I think it makes sense to go that route. Especially with the potential of others helping out. If someone is waiting for a decision, I am willing to make the decision for the group.

My suggestion:
- start the new process on Tuesday, May 7, at the Stan meeting.
- pull request does not guarantee a full code review
- I'll try to get the Jenkins github pull request plugin working. That will allow one of us to kick off the unit tests for the pull request and we can view the results of the tests before the merge.

I've got more below.

On Wed, May 1, 2013 at 4:16 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
On Wednesday, May 1, 2013 3:40:02 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
What I'm wondering is whether we should go
to a system where we pull request rather than
push ourselves and where there's a forced code
review by someone other than the person issuing
the pull request.

I feel that there are a lot of areas of the Stan code that only one person knows well. In that case, the code reviewer might not be able to do that great a job, and the person who has a lot of commits might be slowed down.

Part of the problem is that too many commits are going to the master branch too soon. Like "I'll push the code now and the tests / doc / etc. later". Part of the problem is that we don't enforce a push hook that runs test-unit. I think Bob sent an email a couple of weeks ago about the 5 steps needed to add something to Stan, but we don't really have any formal guidelines.

Unfortunately, I don't think we can run a reasonable post-commit hook through github. The issue is that our unit tests now take 20+ minutes, distribution tests run close to 2 hours, and then another 2 hours for model tests. As of right now, we've got our Jenkins box testing on commits. I wish we could use a post-commit hook, but I don't think we can work that out.

Regarding only one person knowing the code: that shouldn't hold us back from using pull requests.

Should we start managing our TO-DO list as issues? Then individual pull requests would could be tied to things that we want to accomplish.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: new commit/push policy?
parts:
On a bit of a tangent, I'd like to add that the slowness of the tests
is an issue for me running them more often right now. I haven't timed
things but it's slow on my laptop (~3yrs old dual core MacBook Pro,
using clang), definitely more than 20 minutes, probably closer to an
hour. If I've nothing else to do (going to make dinner, whatever)
that's fine, but as a rule it's a burden. A way to have a decent
machine (Jenkins or otherwise) available where I can say "run the for
me" and have it return in a decent amount of time with informative
output would be a big win.

Also, I don't think we need to do formal code review on everything.
Most things probably just need a quick look to catch anything obvious.
It also helps to ensure that more people know what's going on with
different parts of the code.

Finally, we should consider the workflow where not everything gets
done together. E.G., one person writes code, someone else writes the
tests/docs. This has happened a few times for me (thanks Bob!). Does
it all get staged in a different fork before it's finally pulled? I
don't know how hard it is for me to give someone else push access to a
fork on github.

Cheers,
Marcus

On May 1, 2013, at 4:58 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:

Should we start managing our TO-DO list as issues? Then individual pull requests would could be tied to things that we want to accomplish.

I feel that there are a lot of areas of the Stan code that only one person knows well. In that case, the code reviewer might not be able to do that great a job, and the person who has a lot of commits might be slowed down.

While this might slow us down in terms of pull requests, it'd probably be a good idea because then everyone's work would be double checked and sometimes when people review each other's code, some errors or potential improvements will surface. At the same time, I don't think the code review needs to be too rigorous.

And as a side note, I think it would be nice if we had better documentation for testing frameworks (i.e. testing distributions and samplers).


Peter

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: shuffle function_signature tests?
parts:
On Wednesday, May 1, 2013 8:32:01 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
On Wednesday, May 1, 2013 8:15:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Or we need to figure out a way to speed up compilation.
The test execution is fast, but compilation, even using
clang++ -O0 takes a long long time.

At the moment, clang++ swaps a lot on the exp_mod_normal function_signatures and probably the plain normal ones. But most of the time, running test-unit in parallel doesn't take too long on my laptop.

Part of the problem here is that it does the function_signature tests in alphabetical order so all the exp_mod_normal_.*stan functions get parsed, compiled, and run at approximately the same time when using multiple cores in parallel. Would anyone mind if the makefile did a random shuffle (see man shuf for details) of the .stan files under src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/ and looped through the shuffled list? That way, it would be unlikely to get several of the most computationally intensive tests at the same time and thus, unlikely to swap.

Ben

On Sat, May 4, 2013 at 5:12 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

On Wednesday, May 1, 2013 8:32:01 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
On Wednesday, May 1, 2013 8:15:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Or we need to figure out a way to speed up compilation.
The test execution is fast, but compilation, even using
clang++ -O0 takes a long long time.

At the moment, clang++ swaps a lot on the exp_mod_normal function_signatures and probably the plain normal ones. But most of the time, running test-unit in parallel doesn't take too long on my laptop.

Part of the problem here is that it does the function_signature tests in alphabetical order so all the exp_mod_normal_.*stan functions get parsed, compiled, and run at approximately the same time when using multiple cores in parallel. Would anyone mind if the makefile did a random shuffle (see man shuf for details) of the .stan files under src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/ and looped through the shuffled list? That way, it would be unlikely to get several of the most computationally intensive tests at the same time and thus, unlikely to swap.

No, I don't mind. Could you get it working and into the repo?

This patch seems to work for me on Linux and keeps me well under 1GB per processor on average

diff --git a/make/tests b/make/tests
index c1cc03c..e6504f4 100644
--- a/make/tests
+++ b/make/tests
@@ -100,7 +100,7 @@ endif
 ##
 # Builds a single test
 ##
-test/gm/compile_models$(EXE) : test/gm/compile_models.o bin/libstan.a $(patsubst %.stan,%$(EXE),$(wildcard src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/*.stan))
+test/gm/compile_models$(EXE) : test/gm/compile_models.o bin/libstan.a $(shell shuf -e $(patsubst %.stan,%$(EXE),$(wildcard src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/*.stan)))
        @mkdir -p $(dir $@)
        $(LINK.c) -O$O $(GTEST_MAIN) $< $(CFLAGS_GTEST) $(OUTPUT_OPTION) $(LIBGTEST) $(LDLIBS) $(LDLIBS_STANC)
 ifeq ($(findstring test-,$(MAKECMDGOALS))$(findstring runtest/,$(MAKECMDGOALS)),)

Is that likely to work on Windows and / or is there are more canonical way to do it?

Also, I think we should shuffle the test-models so as to avoid doing several multivariate ones at once. Maybe also test-distributions? Perhaps it would be better to ask is there anything in the test suite that you definitely don't want shuffled?

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] shuffle function_signature tests?
parts:
The tests can be shuffled. If not, it's a testing bug.

Daniel -- can you check that this works on Jenkins?

The point is that these are unit tests and should all be independent.
That's why each gets its own executable compiled from scratch.

What we really need to do is attack compile time by putting more
code in precompiled archives. I'd rather wait until the dust
settles on the current refactor/debug before trying to make things
faster, though.

- Bob
